profile.title: Nutrition Counseling for a Guarded Patient with Ischemic Heart Disease and Comfort-Eating Pattern Not Yet Disclosed
profile.summary: This case trains dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment and MI-consistent counseling session with a guarded, low-health-literacy cardiac patient in the preparation stage of change. It emphasizes eliciting a comfort-eating pattern layer by layer (initial minimization, reluctant disclosure, and hidden shame-laden episodes), reconciling a self-reported-versus-record medication adherence mismatch without confrontation, and negotiating one concrete, sustainable dietary change rather than a full overhaul - while correctly disregarding two embedded red herrings (an implausible historical eGFR value and resolved dental work).
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Rockaway, New Jersey, sitting in a cluttered kitchen with the TV audible in the background

patient.name: Abdul Kshlerin
patient.occupation: Maintenance technician at a commercial office building
patient.appearance: Heavyset build, sitting stiffly at a kitchen table in a work polo, partial denture visible when he talks. Posture is closed-off at first—arms crossed, short answers—though he loosens up slightly once rapport builds. The camera shows a crowded kitchen counter behind him with dishes stacked and a coffee maker visible.

persona.personality: Reserved, private, and practical. Measures a good day by staying busy and providing for his family. Prefers logistics-talk ('where to get a decent sandwich') to feelings-talk. Not prone to complaining, slow to warm up but not hostile.
persona.communicationStyle: Gives short, flat answers at first, often one sentence or less. Needs a question asked a second time, gently and in a different way, before he opens up further. Deflects sensitive topics with mild humor or 'it's not a big deal.' Becomes more talkative on neutral/logistics topics (work, food spots, truck) than on feelings or shame-laden topics.
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and a little tired. Not acutely anxious, but carries quiet embarrassment about his eating habits and a mild undercurrent of shame he doesn't name directly. Softens and seems relieved when not judged.
persona.background: Abdul grew up working-class in northern New Jersey and left school after his GED to start working right away. He's been a maintenance technician at a commercial office building for decades, on his feet most of the day fixing things. He lives in a crowded house with his wife, extended family, and visiting grandkids on weekends - seven people under one roof. Food was never a big ritual growing up; whoever got home first ate. As an adult, grabbing takeout became both a convenience and his main way to unwind and connect with coworkers and his wife. On weekends he plays cards with friends at the local VFW hall. He drives a pickup truck for work and often eats lunch in it, parked somewhere quiet.
speechExamples: Eh, I eat out most days. It's just easier with everybody and everything going on.
My wife asks me that enough already.
It's not a big deal. Everybody snacks sometimes.
I don't know, I just want one thing I can actually stick with - not some whole big overhaul.
concerns: Doesn't want another hospital stay that would mean missing work
Doesn't want to be babied or lectured about giving up the one part of his day that feels like his own
Worried his wife hovers too much over what he eats and whether he took his pills
Wants a simple, concrete change, not a long list of things to fix
Doesn't want to be seen as weak or making a big deal out of his health in front of coworkers

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition counseling visit with Abdul Kshlerin, a 66-year-old man with a history of ischemic heart disease and a mechanical aortic valve replacement, referred for nutrition counseling after a recent cardiology follow-up. He has said he wants help figuring out 'one thing' to change about his eating. Review his available health record before or during the call, take a focused diet and lifestyle history, and provide patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referred for nutrition counseling; patient wants to identify one concrete change to his eating
scenario.openingLine: Hey. Yeah, they said I should talk to someone about my eating. I eat out most days - it's just easier with everything going on at home. Figured I'd see what you think I should actually do.
tasks: Take a focused diet and lifestyle history, including meal pattern, food choices, hydration, and physical activity
Review available anthropometric and laboratory data in the chart and relate them to his nutrition status
Explore barriers, beliefs, and readiness to change using open-ended, patient-centered questions
Identify and gently reconcile any inconsistencies between what the patient reports and what the record shows
Negotiate one specific, sustainable first step for dietary change consistent with his stage of readiness, and document your assessment

facts.says: I'm ready to do something. I just want one thing to try, not a whole new way of living.

facts.says: I want to see my grandkids grow up. And I don't want my wife taking care of me like I'm an invalid.

facts.says: Don't tell me to just stop eating out. That's not happening.

facts.chart: Describes eating out and takeout as tied to his main social connection with coworkers and friends
facts.says: Grabbing lunch with the guys, that's kind of my social life. Same with cards at the VFW.

facts.chart: Reports getting winded climbing stairs at the VFW hall where he plays cards weekly
facts.says: Those stairs at the VFW get me huffing lately.

facts.says: I don't love admitting that. Feels kind of pathetic, sitting there alone with a bag of chips at midnight.

actions.result: Patient describes a weekly rotation: diner cheeseburger platter, Chinese takeout (General Tso's chicken, fried rice), pizza near work on Fridays. Reports eating out 'most days, it's just easier.' Says he usually finishes his plate even when full.

actions.name: Screen for physical activity level
actions.result: On his feet most of the workday doing maintenance tasks; no structured exercise program. Reports getting winded climbing stairs at the VFW hall during card games.

actions.name: Screen alcohol and tobacco use
actions.result: Reports 1-2 beers on weekends while playing cards; denies any history of smoking.

actions.name: Assess hydration pattern
actions.result: Patient reports drinking mostly coffee and soda during the day and 'forgets' to drink water.

actions.name: Assess nutrition label literacy and food budget constraints

actions.name: Assess readiness to change (stage-of-change screening)

artifacts.body: 66-year-old male with ischemic heart disease since 2006, aortic valve stenosis since childhood, status post mechanical aortic valve replacement 2019. Stable on current regimen of aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, simvastatin 20 mg nightly, metoprolol succinate ER 100 mg daily, nitroglycerin spray PRN. No new chest pain episodes reported at this visit beyond occasional exertional tightness resolving with rest. Mechanical valve click audible on auscultation, unchanged. Blood pressure runs low at baseline (90s/70s systolic), asymptomatic. Referred to dietetics for nutrition counseling given overweight BMI and reliance on prepared/takeout foods per patient report.

objectives.text: Elicit a full picture of eating patterns—including meal timing, takeout reliance, hydration, and physical activity—in a reserved patient who gives short initial answers, using open-ended and follow-up questioning techniques.
Explore comfort/stress-related eating and shame-laden disclosures without judgment to build trust, recognizing that some information may only surface with repeated, gentle questioning.

Integrate anthropometric and laboratory data into the nutrition assessment, correctly interpreting findings at goal, findings that are stable baseline, and historical values that are inconsistent with the rest of the record.
Identify and gently reconcile a discrepancy between the patient's self-reported medication adherence and objective pharmacy refill data, without confronting or lecturing the patient.
Translate low health-literacy nutrition concepts (sodium, portion size, label reading, cost beliefs) into plain, practical language tailored to the patient's actual food choices.

Negotiate one specific, sustainable first step for dietary change consistent with the patient's preparation stage of readiness, avoiding language implying he must give up eating out, and incorporate the role of his supportive-but-anxious wife while respecting his request for confidentiality.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium and energy intake related to heavy reliance on takeout/convenience foods and emotional (stress/comfort) eating, as evidenced by frequent restaurant/takeout meals, skipped breakfast, late-night snacking episodes, and self-reported stress-driven eating patterns, in a patient with ischemic heart disease and overweight BMI.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive energy/sodium intake related to food/nutrition knowledge deficit and emotional eating
Nutrition diagnosis: Undesirable food choices related to limited access to self-prepared meals (household/budget barriers)
Not primarily a renal nutrition concern - historical eGFR 9.9 (2019) is inconsistent with rest of record and should be flagged for record review, not treated as CKD
Not primarily dental-nutrition related - January dental work is resolved and only caused transient, mild chewing difficulty
keyFindings: BMI 27.8 kg/m2 (overweight), weight 88.1 kg, height 178.1 cm
Lipids at goal 2026-01-05 (TC 133.7, LDL 81.3, TG 117.1) but HDL low at 29.1 mg/dL
Vitals stable baseline: BP 97/75, HR 73, RR 13 - low BP is chronic baseline, no dizziness reported
Diet history: takeout most days (diner, Chinese, pizza Fridays), skipped/rushed breakfast, coffee with cream/sugar multiple cups daily, minimal water intake
Reluctant disclosure: late-night cereal/chip binges 'a few times a week' when stressed or unable to sleep, wakes ~4am
Hidden (may not surface): isolated large-pizza binge last spring with shame afterward; ongoing hidden candy stash in truck glove box eaten alone at lunch
Mismatch: patient reports missing simvastatin only ~once/week, but pharmacy refill record shows refill gaps of 10-14 days beyond a 30-day supply, consistent with more frequent missed doses
Patient in preparation stage of change - wants one concrete swap, not full overhaul; resists framing of 'giving up eating out'

Red herring: eGFR 9.9 mL/min/1.73m2 (2019) is inconsistent with absence of any CKD diagnosis, dialysis, or nephrology follow-up and should be noted as a likely lab/entry error for record review, not pursued as active renal disease
Red herring: recent dental work (fillings/cleaning, Jan 2026) caused brief, now-resolved difficulty chewing; not a current nutritional driver
plan: Complete ADIME-formatted nutrition assessment: diet history, 24-hour recall, meal pattern, hydration, physical activity, psychosocial barriers
Review available anthropometric, vital sign, and lab data already in the chart to contextualize findings (do not duplicate as new findings)
Review pharmacy refill record if available and gently reconcile with patient's self-reported adherence, without accusing or lecturing
Explore late-night eating and stress-related eating patterns using open, non-judgmental, repeated gentle questioning

Negotiate one specific, concrete first step consistent with preparation stage (e.g., a lower-sodium swap at his usual diner, or a specific lunch choice), avoiding language that implies giving up eating out entirely
Provide plain-language education on sodium and portion size using his own food rotation as examples (diner, Chinese takeout, pizza) rather than generic label literacy instruction alone
Explore role of spouse supportively - how she could help without feeling like nagging - while respecting his request for confidentiality about specifics if he asks that details not be shared with her
Document nutrition diagnosis using PES statement and plan for follow-up visit to assess progress on the one agreed change
Flag the eGFR value and refill-gap pattern for review by the broader care team/record reconciliation rather than treating as new diagnoses in this visit
redFlags: Do not initiate or imply new renal diagnosis based on isolated 2019 eGFR of 9.9 without corroborating recent labs or clinical course
Do not confront patient directly or punitively about suspected under-reported statin non-adherence; raise gently and non-judgmentally
Avoid framing counseling as 'give up eating out' - will trigger disengagement given his fear of losing his main social outlet
If patient discloses shame-laden eating episodes, respond without alarm or moralizing to preserve trust and avoid shutting down future disclosure
Respect any explicit request not to relay details of eating behavior to spouse unless there is an immediate safety concern (there is none here)
educationPoints: Simple, concrete swaps within his existing takeout rotation (e.g., smaller portion, lower-sodium order, splitting a meal) are more sustainable for him right now than a full dietary overhaul
Plain-language explanation of how sodium relates to fluid balance and blood pressure, tailored to his usual meals rather than generic label-reading instruction
Reassurance that 'healthy eating' does not require expensive specialty foods - focus on where/how he already eats
Brief, non-alarming explanation linking consistent medication-taking (especially statin) with his heart health, inviting him to raise concerns about side effects with his prescriber
Normalize that stress-related eating is common and not a moral failing, to reduce shame and encourage future openness
Offer one agreed-upon next step and plan to check in on it at a follow-up visit rather than overwhelming him with multiple changes at once

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports taking simvastatin 20 mg nightly, estimates missing it about once a week on late work shifts (h23)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history for simvastatin 20 mg shows refill intervals consistently 10-14 days longer than a 30-day supply would allow, indicating doses are missed more often than reported
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking; refill/fill-date patterns provide objective corroboration and should be reconciled gently without confrontation, especially when nutrition counseling intersects with medication-related risk (e.g., lipid management)

mismatches.patientClaim: States he believes his heart condition is largely resolved since the valve surgery (h9/s7)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Cardiology follow-up note documents ongoing ischemic heart disease since 2006 and aortic valve stenosis since 1963 as active, longstanding diagnoses with no indication of resolution, only absence of new acute events since last follow-up
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may misunderstand chronic disease as 'fixed' after a procedure; clarifying this belief (without alarming the patient) is relevant to framing nutrition counseling as part of ongoing cardiac risk management rather than optional lifestyle advice
